# Exploratory data analysis {#eda}

**Exploratory data analysis** (EDA), a term introduced by John W. Tukey, is the detective work done before any formal test or model. Its purpose is to get to know the data: check that they were entered correctly, see how each variable is distributed, find unusual observations and discover relationships worth testing. EDA combines the summaries of Chapter \@ref(descriptive-statistics) with the graphs of Chapter \@ref(graphical-representation).

A useful checklist:

1. Check the structure: number of rows and columns, variable types, factor levels.
2. Look for missing values and data-entry errors.
3. Summarise and plot each variable (univariate analysis).
4. Summarise and tabulate by groups.
5. Look for outliers.
6. Check the shape of the distributions (symmetry, normality) and consider transformations.
7. Examine relationships between variables (bivariate and multivariate analysis).

## The example data

We use the `plrv` data from the `agricolae` package. The International Potato Center (CIP), Peru, evaluated 28 potato genotypes (clones from a population selected for resistance to potato leaf roll virus, plus the check varieties Canchan, Desiree and Unica) in six environments, with three replications each. Tuber yield (t/ha) and weights per plant and per plot (kg) were recorded.

```{r eda-data}
library(agricolae)
data(plrv)
```

## Structure of the data

```{r eda-str}
dim(plrv)
str(plrv)
head(plrv)
```

`Rep` is stored as an integer, but it identifies replications, so it should be a factor:

```{r eda-factor}
plrv$Rep <- factor(plrv$Rep)
nlevels(plrv$Genotype)
levels(plrv$Locality)
```

## Missing values and data checks

```{r eda-missing}
sum(is.na(plrv))          # total number of missing values
colSums(is.na(plrv))      # missing values per column
```

There are no missing values. Next check that the design is balanced, i.e. every genotype appears once in every replication of every locality:

```{r eda-balance}
table(plrv$Locality, plrv$Rep)
all(table(plrv$Genotype, plrv$Locality) == 3)
```

Each locality has 28 plots per replication and every genotype has three plots in each locality, so the data are complete and balanced. Also look for impossible values, such as negative yields:

```{r eda-range}
range(plrv$Yield)
```

## Univariate analysis

```{r eda-summary}
summary(plrv$Yield)
```

```{r eda-hist, fig.asp=0.5, fig.width=9}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(plrv$Yield, col = "#D6EAF8", border = "white",
     main = "Histogram of yield", xlab = "Yield (t/ha)")
boxplot(plrv$Yield, horizontal = TRUE, col = "#FAD7A0",
        main = "Box plot of yield", xlab = "Yield (t/ha)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The distribution is skewed to the right, with a long tail of high yields. A **stem-and-leaf plot** shows the same shape while keeping the actual values:

```{r eda-stem}
stem(round(plrv$Yield))
```

## Tabulation and summaries by group

### Frequency and contingency tables

`table()` counts observations in each category; with two factors it gives a contingency (two-way) table. `xtabs()` does the same with a formula, and `prop.table()` converts counts to proportions. Here yields are first grouped into classes with `cut()`:

```{r eda-tab}
plrv$YieldClass <- cut(plrv$Yield, breaks = c(0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 100),
                       labels = c("<10", "10-20", "20-30", "30-40", ">40"))
tab <- xtabs(~ Locality + YieldClass, data = plrv)
tab

# Row percentages: distribution of yield classes within each locality
round(prop.table(tab, margin = 1) * 100, 1)

# Add row and column totals
addmargins(tab)
```

### Summary statistics by group

`aggregate()` computes any function for each group. Here we compute the mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of yield in each locality:

```{r eda-agg}
cv <- function(x) sd(x) / mean(x) * 100
loc_stats <- aggregate(Yield ~ Locality, data = plrv,
                       FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), cv = cv(x)))
loc_stats <- do.call(data.frame, loc_stats)
names(loc_stats) <- c("Locality", "Mean", "SD", "CV")
loc_stats[order(-loc_stats$Mean), ]
```

Mean yields range from about `r round(min(loc_stats$Mean), 1)` t/ha to `r round(max(loc_stats$Mean), 1)` t/ha across environments. A two-way table of means by genotype and locality is obtained with `tapply()`:

```{r eda-twoway}
gl <- with(plrv, tapply(Yield, list(Genotype, Locality), mean))
round(head(gl), 1)
```

and the best and worst genotypes over all environments are:

```{r eda-geno}
g <- sort(tapply(plrv$Yield, plrv$Genotype, mean), decreasing = TRUE)
round(head(g, 5), 2)
round(tail(g, 3), 2)
```

### Graphs by group

```{r eda-box-loc}
boxplot(Yield ~ Locality, data = plrv, col = "#A9DFBF",
        ylab = "Yield (t/ha)", xlab = "Environment")
```

The box plot shows that most of the variation in yield comes from differences **between environments**. The right skew seen in the overall histogram is largely the result of mixing environments with very different mean yields.

An **interaction plot** shows whether genotypes rank similarly in all environments. Here we plot the three check varieties:

```{r eda-interaction}
checks <- droplevels(subset(plrv, Genotype %in% c("Canchan", "Desiree", "Unica")))
with(checks, interaction.plot(Locality, Genotype, Yield,
     col = c("red", "blue", "darkgreen"), lwd = 2, ylab = "Mean yield (t/ha)"))
```

The lines are not parallel, which suggests **genotype × environment interaction**: the varieties do not respond in the same way in every environment.

## Outliers

The box-plot rule (Chapter \@ref(graphical-representation)) flags as outliers the observations beyond $Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR}$ and $Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}$:

```{r eda-out}
out <- boxplot.stats(plrv$Yield)$out
plrv[plrv$Yield %in% out, c("Genotype", "Locality", "Rep", "Yield")]
```

All four come from LM-03, the highest-yielding environment. Outliers should be judged **within** the relevant group. A common rule standardises each value within its group ($z$-score) and flags observations with $|z| > 3$:

```{r eda-z}
z <- ave(plrv$Yield, plrv$Locality, FUN = function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x))
plrv[abs(z) > 3, c("Genotype", "Locality", "Yield")]
```

No observation is more than three standard deviations from its environment mean, so the four "outliers" are not unusual once the environment is taken into account.

::: {.rmdwarning}
Never delete an outlier just because it is extreme. First check the field book for a recording or data-entry error. Remove or correct a value only if there is a documented reason, and report what was done.
:::

## Checking normality

Many tests and ANOVA assume normally distributed errors. A **normal Q–Q plot** plots the ordered data against the quantiles expected from a normal distribution; normal data fall close to a straight line.

```{r eda-qq, fig.asp=0.5, fig.width=9}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(plrv$Yield, main = "Yield: all environments"); qqline(plrv$Yield, col = "red")
ayac <- plrv$Yield[plrv$Locality == "Ayac"]
qqnorm(ayac, main = "Yield: Ayacucho only"); qqline(ayac, col = "red")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The **Shapiro–Wilk test** tests the null hypothesis that the data come from a normal distribution:

```{r eda-shapiro}
shapiro.test(plrv$Yield)
shapiro.test(ayac)
```

Pooled over all environments, yield is clearly not normal ($p < 0.001$). Within Ayacucho the test gives $p =$ `r round(shapiro.test(ayac)$p.value, 3)`. In a designed experiment, normality is assessed on the **residuals** of the fitted model, not on the raw data (Chapter \@ref(anova-crd)).

### Transformations

When data are skewed or the variance increases with the mean, a transformation can help:

| Type of data | Transformation | R code |
|:-------------|:---------------|:-------|
| Counts (insects, lesions, weeds) | square root | `sqrt(x)` or `sqrt(x + 0.5)` |
| Percentages or proportions (germination, disease incidence) | angular (arcsine) | `asin(sqrt(p))` with `p` = proportion |
| Positive data with variance ∝ mean² (yield, biomass, income) | logarithmic | `log(x)` or `log(x + 1)` |

See Chapter 7 of @gomez1984 for guidance. The Box–Cox procedure (`MASS::boxcox()`) can suggest a suitable power transformation.

## Relationships between variables

A scatter-plot matrix and a correlation matrix give a first view of the relationships among several numeric variables:

```{r eda-pairs, fig.asp=0.8}
pairs(plrv[, c("WeightPlant", "WeightPlot", "Yield")],
      col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.5), pch = 19)
round(cor(plrv[, c("WeightPlant", "WeightPlot", "Yield")]), 3)
```

Plot weight and yield are almost perfectly correlated (r = `r round(cor(plrv$WeightPlot, plrv$Yield), 3)`), as expected, because yield per hectare is calculated from plot weight. The `corrplot` package draws a correlation matrix as a picture, which is useful when there are many variables:

```{r eda-corrplot, fig.asp=0.8, out.width="65%"}
library(corrplot)
data(yacon)
corrplot(cor(yacon[, c("height", "stalks", "roots", "FOS", "brix", "foliage", "dry", "IH")]),
         method = "ellipse", type = "upper", diag = FALSE)
```

Chapter \@ref(regression) covers correlation in detail.

## Exercises {-}

::: {.rmdexercise}
1. Carry out an exploratory data analysis of the `yacon` data in `agricolae`: check its structure, summarise dry root matter (`roots`) by locality and fertiliser dose, and draw suitable graphs.
2. Make a two-way table of mean `brix` by `entry` and `locality`. Which entry has the highest mean?
3. Draw a normal Q–Q plot of `roots` for each locality. Is the distribution approximately normal within localities?
4. The `InsectSprays` data give counts of insects after six insecticide treatments. Draw box plots of `count` and of `sqrt(count)` by `spray`. What does the square-root transformation do to the spread within groups?
:::
